source.title: Generalization error of minimum weighted norm and kernel interpolation

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies minimum weighted-norm trigonometric interpolation rather than deep-network scaling. Its own numerical experiments sweep the number of parameters and report test-error curves, conceptually testing whether generalization can improve again past interpolation.
record.gate_note: The numerical error curves and the reported change in the best over-parameterized smoothness choice as sample count increases are included. Claims about double descent cited from other work are not treated as this study's results. The plotted curves provide no exact numeric error values.
record.test_reason: The study gives its own experiments and theory on V4 for a non-deep model class: trigonometric least squares for p≤n and minimum weighted-norm interpolation for p>n. Corollary 3.2 and Theorem 4.2 state when error does or does not fall again past interpolation. It neither replicates nor starts from the deep-network setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors prove that minimum weighted-norm interpolants converge, as p grows, to the RKHS kernel interpolant, and that error converges to its error (the plateau). Whether over-parameterization helps or hurts depends on whether this plateau is small. That in turn depends on sampling density, target regularity and weight. They also give plateau bounds for trigonometric, spherical-harmonic and NTK cases.
record.recipe_differences: The paper gives deterministic approximation-theoretic analysis and a trigonometric-polynomial numerical illustration, rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments. It uses weighted-norm interpolation for p>n and least squares for p≤n.
record.method_sensitivity: The over-parameterized error depends on smoothness weight s. The best p→∞ smoothness choice changes from s=4 at n=35, to s=3 at n=105, to s=2 at n=205; the text says increasing n decreases the plateau.

fits_no_version.finding: With n=35, 105, 205 samples the p→∞ plateau decreases with n, and the best smoothness s shifts from 4 to 3 to 2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In minimum-norm trigonometric interpolation, more samples lower the over-parameterized plateau, and the best implicit-bias norm depends on sample density relative to target regularity.

record.peer_reviewed: SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science
record.problems: The numerical evidence concerns one target function and one-dimensional trigonometric polynomials. Curves are reported only in figures without exact error values or stated uncertainty intervals; averages use 100 random sampling-set realizations.

untested.parts: Deep networks are not studied; only trigonometric and spherical-harmonic interpolation.
Error over training epochs is not studied.
Sample count is varied (n=35,105,205), but only the p→∞ plateau is discussed, not whether more data raises error near p≈n.
Only 1-D trigonometric interpolation of the Runge function is tested numerically. Other model classes are covered by theory only (spherical harmonics, NTK), with no experiments.
No effective-complexity predictor of peak location is tested.
Noiseless samples and ridgeless interpolation only. There is no label-noise sweep, no tuned regularization, and no multiple-descent test.

missing.what: Theoretical result: minimum weighted-norm interpolants converge to the kernel interpolant as p→∞, and error converges to a plateau. Over-parameterization lowers error only if the plateau is below the error at p=p_X, and can raise it otherwise. Upper bounds on the plateau are given for the torus, sphere and NTK.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Its numerical evidence is figure-only, a single target function, 1-D. The peak at p≈n is attributed to poor conditioning (citing Poggio et al.), not to noise; the samples are noiseless.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network model-size double descent; experiments use trigonometric polynomials.
Error over training epochs or training time.
The sample-count experiments discuss the p→∞ plateau, not whether more data raises error near the interpolation threshold.
Only one-dimensional trigonometric interpolation and a particular Runge-function experiment are studied; other model classes and broad generality are not tested.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across axes.
No label-noise sweep, multiple/triple-descent test, or optimally tuned regularization test is reported.
No re-counting of complexity by an effective number of parameters is tested.
